blocks: Flasch, an electronics specialist. Mr. Flasch used a variac and heavy-duty transformer run through a full-wave rectifier and capacitive filters to deliver up to 1300 V of DC power. However, upon further investigation by Prof. Peshkin, the source proved extremely dangerous. Criteria for “dangerous” are as follows.

Due to the use of capacitive filters, the worst-case scenario involves a full discharge of the capacitors into the researcher. Using the capacitive energy formula, the variac driven source would discharge 750 Joules. Prof. Peshkin uses the rule of thumb that 25 joules will kill a person. Thus, the original set-up, if discharged directly into a person, would kill them 30 times over. Obviously, this High Voltage source was scrapped.

Emco sources were decided upon instead. The selected E20 series provides a proportional output of 0 – 2000V DC from an input of 0-12 V DC. The source is safe since it only uses four 0.845 μF capacitors for filtering and therefore can only discharge (.5)(.845*4*10⁻⁶ F)(1000² V) = 1.7 Joules. While 1.7 Joules is not fatal, it could potentially cause injury. In order to achieve the safest source possible, plans for a box to contain the source and all associated circuitry were realized.

In this circuit, a voltage divider composed of two 10 MΩ resistors and one 200 KΩ is used to create lower voltages in order to prevent the overload of the digital voltmeter that would be used for monitoring. One must simply multiply the voltmeter reading by 100 to obtain the voltage being exerted on the EAP. The two 100 KΩ resistors provide another degree of safety, as they act as fuses that would disintegrate from the sudden current surge that a high voltage discharge would create. All these components, along with appropriate input wiring and interconnects were successfully assembled into a metal box. The high voltage source did test properly and delivered high voltages while the voltmeter reading was in fact 100 times lower.

The mechanical aspect of the fixture stretches the polymer in the horizontal direction (pre-strain) while allowing it freedom to actuate in the vertical direction. This tapestry-like hanging was accomplished using a simple Lexan base and stand. Aluminum was then employed for its malleable properties to provide the top and bottom bracket supports. Specifically, tapped holes were put into the front face of each of these principal brackets. Screws were then run into these holes to provide the squeezing force necessary to secure the elastic material. The screws were a horizontal distance of 3 inches away from each other. This provides 300% pre-strain for a one inch width of tape. Though effective, the top and bottom brackets can only pre-strain the material directly at the top and bottom of the sheet, thus causing the intermediate polymer to shrink back on itself. To counter act this behavior, a series of copper welding rods were cut to size and glued as ribs to the surface of the VHB as it was completely pre-strained in a rigid frame. Once the frame was cut away, the VHB retained its pre-strain throughout and achieved the original aim of pre-strain with freedom of movement in the direction normal to the pre-strain.

Initially, the complex mechanical apparatus was hooked up to the 2kV high voltage source. Unfortunately, all observers present perceived no movement upon application of 2kV. This failure could have been caused by various factors. First, the mechanical set-up is exceedingly complicated. As mentioned above, the device pre-strained the 1 in wide tape 300% to 3 in and used glued copper welding rods for support. This glue becomes very stiff when set and effectively became a stiff overcoat on the VHB that could have constricted any motion. Additional aspects of the complex design most likely contributed to the failure, but the “glue” hypothesis seems to be the biggest factor. In any case, this first design was scrapped.

In order to avoid the repetition of the above mistakes associated with complexity, Professor Colgate suggested simplifying the apparatus to something akin to Figure 3. This configuration essentially simplifies the EAP to its fundamental structure, two compliant electrodes that impose Maxwell stresses (through application of voltage) on an intermediary polymer (VHB 4910). Here the pre-strain is achieved by simply stretching the VHB uniformly over a rigid frame, thus creating a “drum” like set-up.
